title: Debugging Running Containers: A Dense-Notes Field Guide
summary: A study-notes handbook on debugging live containers: exec and logs, healthchecks, resource limits, cgroup internals, and namespace inspection — mechanics, commands, trade-offs, and classic mistakes.

chapters.title: Ch 1 — The Debugging Mindset for Containers
points: Container = process wrapped in namespaces + cgroups; debugging is really debugging a process with an isolated view
Ephemeral by design: containers die and restart with fresh filesystems — persist state via volumes before deep debugging
Debug surface layers: process (exec), stdout/stderr (logs), liveness (healthchecks), resources (cgroups), isolation (namespaces)
Rule: never 'fix' a running container by hand; reproduce, fix the image/config, redeploy
Container != VM: no full init system, no systemd usually, shared kernel with host
PID 1 in a container is your app (or entrypoint) — no reapster for zombies unless tini/init is used
Is the container running but broken, restarting, or crashing? docker ps STATUS column tells you which path to take
docker ps -a to see exited containers; docker start/attach to re-enter a stopped one
Exit codes are diagnostics: 137 = SIGKILL (OOM often), 143 = SIGTERM, 126/127 = command/exec problems
Immutable-image philosophy: a 'fixed' running container is a drift bomb; changes vanish on restart
Ask first: is it the container, the orchestrator, or the host? Check docker inspect vs kubectl describe vs dmesg
Debug toolkit map: docker logs → docker exec → docker inspect → docker stats → nsenter/proc

chapters.title: Ch 2 — docker exec: Into the Live Process
points: docker exec runs a NEW process inside the container's existing namespaces — it does not 'enter' the main process
Syntax: docker exec -it <ctr> sh — prefer sh over bash; slim images often lack bash
-i keeps STDIN open, -t allocates a TTY; without -t output loses colors/prompt but works in scripts
exec vs attach: attach attaches to PID 1's stdio (and a Ctrl-C can kill your app); exec spawns a side process — safer
Use exec --user to test permission problems: docker exec -it --user 1000:1000 <ctr> sh
Env is inherited from container config; exec -e VAR=x to probe env-dependent bugs
If the image has no shell (distroless): docker debug (podman), ephemeral debug containers (kubectl debug), or cp a static busybox in
Exit code of exec = exit code of the command run — scriptable health probes: docker exec <ctr> test -f /tmp/ready
Non-interactive one-liners for probing: docker exec <ctr> ps aux, cat /etc/resolv.conf, env
Gotcha: exec won't start if the container is restarting/crash-looping — debug via logs or run an identical container on the same volume instead
exec'd processes appear in docker top and host ps — remember when auditing
Write permission tests: docker exec <ctr> touch /data/probe && docker exec <ctr> rm /data/probe

chapters.title: Ch 3 — Logs: stdout, stderr, and the Logging Driver
points: Docker captures container stdout+stderr as JSON lines (default json-file driver) stored under /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log
docker logs -f <ctr> = tail -f; --tail 100 for recent; --since/--until for time windows
Add timestamps with -t; this exposes lag between log time and real event time
Logs only capture what the app writes to fd 1/2 — files written inside the container are NOT in docker logs (common trap with nginx/app writing to /var/log)
Redirect in-process (symlink access.log → /dev/stdout) or run tail -F in the container to forward file logs to stdout
docker logs fails with 'unrecognized log driver' when using journald/fluentd/syslog drivers — use the driver's own tooling
Log rotation: default json-file driver has NO size limit — set --log-opt max-size/max-file or disk fills silently
json-file shows partial lines: long lines are split with 'partial': true markers
Multi-line logs (stack traces) pollute JSON lines — handle in the collector (fluentd multiline parser), not at the source
Orchestration: kubectl logs <pod> -c <container>; -p for previous crashed container's logs — gold for crash loops
Correlating logs: log the container ID/hostname and request ID at startup to join app logs with infra logs
Trade-off: logging to stdout = simple and centralized, but loses per-file structure; pick per component, not per platform

chapters.title: Ch 4 — Healthchecks: Knowing Broken vs Alive
points: HEALTHCHECK in Dockerfile or --health-* flags define a probe; states: starting → healthy / unhealthy
HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -f http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1 — nonzero exit = failed check
Tuning: --interval 30s, --timeout 5s, --start-period 40s, --retries 3 — start-period prevents boot-time false kills
docker inspect --format='{{json .State.Health}}' <ctr> shows status, failing streak, and last probe output+exit code — the key debug output
docker events --filter event=health_status streams unhealthy transitions live
Healthcheck ≠ liveness kill in plain Docker: Docker marks it unhealthy but does nothing; orchestrators restart/route based on it
Kubernetes splits it: livenessProbe (restart), readinessProbe (traffic), startupProbe (boot grace) — one probe is rarely enough
Cheap probes without curl in minimal images: exec an app subcommand, test a unix socket with [ -S ], or wget --spider
Probe cost: a health endpoint hitting the DB on every check turns probes into load generators — cache or shallow-check
Gotcha: exec-form probes with shell || exit 1 semantics vs CMD-SHELL form; shell form needed for pipes/||
Readiness should gate traffic, liveness only detect unrecoverable states — a failing dependency belongs in readiness, not liveness (else restart storm)
Anti-pattern: checking the process exists (pgrep) — a wedged process is 'alive'; probe behavior, not existence

chapters.title: Ch 5 — Resource Limits: CPU and Memory Flags
points: --memory (hard cap): exceeding it → OOM kill (exit 137); --memory-swap caps RAM+swap (memory-swap = memory means no swap)
--cpus=1.5 (CFS quota, modern) vs --cpu-shares (relative weight, only enforced under contention)
--cpuset-cpus pins to specific cores — useful for NUMA/latency-sensitive workloads
CPU limits don't kill; they throttle → symptoms are latency spikes and timeouts, not crashes — very different debug signature than memory
docker stats: live CPU%, MEM usage vs limit, net/block IO per container — first tool for 'is it resource pressure?'
docker stats shows the swap illusion: MEM USE includes cache; compare against limit, not host RAM
Throttle detection: /sys/fs/cgroup cpu.stat inside the container — nr_throttled and throttled_time are the smoking gun
Memory fields: memory.usage_in_bytes vs memory.max; events (v2) or memory.failcnt (v1) count limit hits
JVM and similar runtimes need explicit heap settings — old 'read host RAM' heuristics mis-size the container
Limit trade-off: no limits = noisy neighbor; tight limits = OOM kills and throttling — size from measured peaks (docker stats / metrics), plus ~20% headroom
Gotcha: --memory without --memory-swap still allows swap = 2× apparent limit; surprising slowness comes from swap-in
In Kubernetes: requests (scheduling) vs limits (enforcement) — CPU-only requests, or Guaranteed QoS when limits = requests

chapters.title: Ch 6 — cgroups Internals: How Limits Are Enforced
points: cgroups (control groups) are a kernel feature that accounts and limits CPU, memory, IO, pids per group of processes
Two versions: cgroup v1 (one hierarchy per controller, /sys/fs/cgroup/<ctl>) vs v2 (unified tree, /sys/fs/cgroup/<ctr>.scope) — check with stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup (cgroup2fs = v2)
CPU enforcement = CFS bandwidth: cpu.max = 'quota period' (v2), e.g. '150000 100000' = 1.5 CPUs; cfs_quota_us/cfs_period_us in v1
cpu.stat: nr_periods, nr_throttled, throttled_usec — throttled close to periods means your limit is the bottleneck
Memory: memory.max (hard), memory.high (soft throttle via reclaim before OOM), memory.current (usage)
OOM path: hitting memory.max → kernel OOM killer picks largest RSS in the group → SIGKILL, exit 137; find it in dmesg or memory.events oom_kill counter
Page cache counts toward memory.current — a container streaming big files can OOM on cache, not heap; kernel reclaims it but can spike past high
pids.max controller caps fork bombs: 'fork: Cannot allocate memory' when pids exhausted, not RAM
Find a container's cgroup: /proc/<pid>/cgroup on the host, or docker inspect .Id → /sys/fs/cgroup/.../docker-<id>.scope
Hierarchy inheritance: limits set on a parent (e.g. pod slice) constrain all children — k8s pod-level limits live above container scopes
Debug trick: cat the cgroup files from inside the container (they're its view) — no host access needed for cpu.stat/memory.max
v1↔v2 gotcha: tutorials' v1 paths fail on modern distros; know both names (cfs_quota_us ↔ cpu.max, memory.limit_in_bytes ↔ memory.max)

chapters.title: Ch 7 — Namespaces: What the Container Sees
points: Namespaces virtualize kernel views; a container = usual Linux process with a stack of namespaces
Core set: PID, NET, MNT, UTS (hostname), IPC, USER, CGROUP, (TIME newer) — each isolates one dimension
PID namespace: container sees its own process numbering starting at 1; host sees real PIDs — that's why host ps shows more
NET namespace: private interfaces, routes, iptables, ports; docker0 bridge + veth pair connect container to host
MNT namespace: private mount table — /proc inside shows container mounts; bind mounts appear in both views
USER namespace: maps container UIDs to host UIDs (root in container = unprivileged on host, with userns-remap/rootless)
Inspect from inside: ls /proc/*/ns/, readlink /proc/self/ns/<ns> gives per-namespace inode — equal inode = same namespace
Inspect from host: lsns -t pid,net lists namespaces and their processes; pid's /proc/<pid>/ns links are your entry
Real PIDs from host: docker top <ctr> maps container PIDs to host PIDs — needed for strace/perf from host
Debug via proc even without a shell in the image: from host, /proc/<hostpid>/root/ is the container filesystem, /proc/<hostpid>/cmdline its command
Sharing namespaces: docker run --pid=host / --network=host breaks isolation for debugging (or reuse another container's: --network=container:<x>)
Gotcha: two containers on the same network (k8s pod) share NET but not PID namespaces — localhost works, ps doesn't

chapters.title: Ch 8 — nsenter, /proc, and Host-Side Deep Inspection
points: nsenter -t <hostpid> -n -p -m sh enters a process's namespaces from the host — works when exec can't (no shell image, agent-based tooling)
Flag map: -p PID ns, -n net, -m mount, -i IPC, -u UTS, -U user; omit flags you don't need
Get host PID first: docker inspect --format '{{.State.Pid}}' <ctr>, or crictl inspect in k8s
Host PID namespace view: ps aux | grep <ctr-id-prefix> — host PID 12345 = container PID N
strace a container process from host: nsenter -t <pid> -p strace -p <inner_pid> — or strace directly on host PID, syscall table is shared
net tools in net ns: nsenter -t <pid> -n ss -tlnp, ip addr — check listening ports/DNS routes without exec
Check open files/fds: ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd and fd/... → detects leaked sockets, deleted-but-open logs (disk not freed)
/proc/<pid>/status: NSpid line shows the PID translation chain across namespace layers
k8s equivalent: kubectl debug node/<node> -it --image=busybox, then nsenter -t 1 -... or crictl ps/plogs for crash-looping pods
Warning: entering mnt+pid ns of a live container and mutating things = debugging via production surgery; prefer read-only inspection
crash-loop trick: docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh --volumes-from <crashed> <image> to explore its volumes with a shell
tcpdump in the net ns from host captures container traffic without installing anything in the image

chapters.title: Ch 9 — docker inspect and the Metadata Goldmine
points: docker inspect <ctr> dumps full config+state JSON — the ground truth of what actually runs, not what you think runs
Compare intent vs reality: diff .Config.Cmd/.Entrypoint/.Env against the Dockerfile/compose file — drift is a top bug source
State block: Status, Pid, ExitCode, OOMKilled (bool!), StartedAt, RestartCount, Health — OOMKilled=true instantly explains exit 137
NetworkSettings: IPAddress, Ports (mapped host:container), Networks — resolves 'why can't I connect' half the time
Mounts array: source → destination, mode (rw/ro) — wrong mount path/mode explains permission and missing-file bugs
Format queries: docker inspect -f '{{.State.Health.Status}}' / '{{range .Mounts}}{{.Source}} {{end}}' — scriptable, no jq needed (but jq is fine too)
RestartPolicy + RestartCount: On-failure loops hide flaky crashes; inspect restart history before logs get rotated away
Image vs container: docker image inspect for labels, layers, history — docker history shows layer-by-layer commands and sizes
docker inspect also works on images/volumes/networks — same tool, different objects
docker events --since 1h: full lifecycle audit (start, die, oom, health_status, kill with signal) — reconstruct the timeline of a crash
docker port <ctr> and docker diff <ctr> (filesystem changes vs image) — docker diff exposes hand-fixes/drift inside the running container
Machine-readable everything: pair inspect JSON with docker stats --no-stream in scripts for a point-in-time debug snapshot

chapters.title: Ch 10 — Field Guide: Symptoms → Tools → Fixes (Summary)
points: Crash loop → docker logs -p (k8s) or logs of previous container + .State.ExitCode/OOMKilled from inspect; fix image/config, not the running instance
Exit 137 + OOMKilled=true → raise memory limit or fix leak; verify via memory.current vs memory.max and oom events in dmesg
Slow but alive → check cpu.stat nr_throttled/throttled_usec; CPU limits throttle, memory limits kill — different symptoms, same cgroup system
App up but unreachable → inspect NetworkSettings/Ports, nsenter -t <pid> -n ss -tlnp: is it listening on 0.0.0.0 or only 127.0.0.1?
Logs empty → app writes to files not stdout; symlink to /dev/stdout or run with a tail sidecar
Exec says 'container not running' during crash loop → recreate with changed entrypoint (sleep infinity) or debug from host via nsenter
'Healthy' but broken → probe checks existence not behavior; rewrite healthcheck to exercise a real code path
Works locally, dies in prod → compare docker inspect .Config/.Env and cgroup limits between environments; drift lives in config
Disk filling → json-file log driver without max-size rotation; or deleted-but-open files in /proc/<pid>/fd
Zombie processes accumulating → PID 1 isn't reaping; add tini/--init
Method recap: status → logs → inspect → exec/stats → cgroups → namespaces; outside-in, read-only before surgery
Golden rules: treat containers as cattle, capture evidence (inspect/events/logs) before touching, and always fix at the image/config layer
